issues.issue: Relief turns on conditions that "differ materially" from those indicated, or unknown conditions "of an unusual nature" differing materially from those ordinarily found, none of which is defined or measured. Whether a given site condition qualifies is a pure question of construction.

The clause lists six specific grounds for additional-cost claims and then adds "(7) other reasonable grounds," leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain against the enumerated specifics. Whether it is confined to grounds of the same kind is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

Weather claims require data showing conditions were "abnormal for the period of time, could not have been reasonably anticipated and had an adverse effect," with no baseline stated for abnormality. On a Hawaii project the benchmark is left entirely open.

The provision operates on "unit prices stated in the Contract Documents," but Subparagraph 5.2.3 of the Agreement leaves the unit-price slot blank. There are no unit prices for the equitable-adjustment mechanism to apply to.

The mutual waiver of "consequential damages" is followed by illustrative lists and a saving for "liquidated direct damages," leaving the line between waived consequential loss and recoverable direct loss undrawn. Which side of the line delay or completion costs fall on is a construction question.

The waiver is said to apply "without limitation, to all consequential damages due to either party's termination in accordance with Article 14," yet 14.1.3 lets a terminating Contractor recover "reasonable overhead, profit and damages" and 14.4.3 allows overhead and profit on Work not executed. The two provisions pull in opposite directions on termination recovery.

The Architect's initial decision is made "a condition precedent to mediation, arbitration or litigation of all Claims ... unless 30 days have passed after the Claim has been referred to the Architect with no decision having been rendered." Whether a party that never referred a Claim is barred, and how the proviso interacts with the bar, is left to construction.

This condition precedent sits against Subparagraph 12.2.4 of the Agreement, which lets the Contractor demand arbitration of the final accounting "without a further decision of the Architect." The instrument gives two different routes to arbitration.

The Architect's approval or rejection of a Claim is stated to be "final and binding on the parties but subject to mediation and arbitration," which are two inconsistent characterisations in one sentence. What the decision binds, and to what effect in a later proceeding, is unclear.

The 30-day demand rule operates only when the Architect's written decision "states" both of two things, and the consequence of failing to demand within 30 days — the decision becoming final and binding — is expressed in text that is partly broken here. Whether a decision triggered the deadline is left to construction.

Mediation is made "a condition precedent to arbitration or the institution of legal or equitable proceedings," subject to exceptions for aesthetic effect and waived Claims, with the Architect's decision or 30 days' delay as the starting point. Whether suit is barred by a failure to mediate, and which Claims escape, are both live on these words.

The arbitration agreement covers "any Claim arising out of or related to the Contract" except aesthetic-effect Claims and those waived under 4.3.10, 9.10.4 and 9.10.5, and is conditioned on the Architect's initial decision or 30 days' delay. The scope of the exceptions and the effect of the condition are the classic points of dispute, and the text here is partly garbled.

The outer limit is the date when "institution of legal or equitable proceedings based on such Claim would be barred by the applicable statute of limitations as determined pursuant to Paragraph 13.7," which requires layering a contractual accrual rule onto a statutory period. When a demand is too late is not readable from the clause alone.

Joinder is permitted only of persons "substantially involved in a common question of fact or law whose presence is required if complete relief is to be accorded," and excluded where the interest or responsibility is "insubstantial." Both tests are undefined and decide who may be brought into the arbitration.

The demanding party "must assert in the demand all Claims then known to that party," but the provision states no consequence for omitting one. Whether omitted Claims are waived is not answered by the words.

The Architect-and-Owner approval route for proposed subcontractors overlaps Article 10.1 of the Agreement, under which the Contractor delivers bids and "the Owner shall then determine, with the advice of the Contractor and the Architect, which bids will be accepted." Two different selection procedures are provided.

A Change Order is defined as an instrument signed by Owner, Contractor and Architect, while the Addendum's Section 6.5 says a Change Order "shall be issued" whenever a Schedule of Values price is refined and 3.10.5 makes revised estimates part of the Contract Documents without signature. The formalities do not match.

The subparagraph survives only as a broken fragment ("determining adjustments to the Contract Sum may include those listed"), so the methods it refers to cannot be identified from the text. What it provides is unreadable.

The Architect must fix the adjustment "on the basis of reasonable expenditures and savings," and the enumerated cost categories close with "additional costs of supervision and field office personnel directly attributable to the change." Both the reasonableness standard and the closed list's reach are open to argument.

The Architect's power to order minor changes binding on the Owner is in tension with Supplementary Condition 1.2.1.1(c), which requires Owner and Architect approval of minor field changes, and with 1.1.2.1, which requires the Owner's express written concurrence wherever the Architect acts. Whether the Architect alone can bind the Owner is unsettled.

Contract Time is defined as a "period of time ... allotted in the Contract Documents" for Substantial Completion, but revised Article 4.3 fixes completion by a calendar date rather than a period, and original 4.3's day-count is incomplete. The measure of the Contract Time is not consistently expressed.

This treats the date of commencement as "the date established in the Agreement," while Article 4.1 gives only an approximate July date and revised 4.1 makes it July 15, 2002 "pending approval of permits." No single established date exists.

After enumerating specific delay causes the clause adds "other causes beyond the Contractor's control" and "other causes which the Architect determines may justify delay," so the reach of the catch-alls against the listed specifics is uncertain. The extension is also left to whatever the Architect "may determine."

This says "the Contract Sum is stated in the Agreement," but the Agreement states no sum: 5.1.1 defines it as the Cost of the Work plus the Fee and 5.2.1 fills the Guaranteed Maximum Price in as "N/A." The total amount payable is nowhere stated.

This schedule-of-values provision requires allocation of the Contract Sum, while Subparagraph 12.1.5 of the Agreement requires allocation of "the entire Guaranteed Maximum Price," which is stated as "N/A." The two allocation bases differ.
